source_document.body:
I spent my early career working on space systems at Los Angeles Air Force Base: satellite technology, space defense infrastructure—the kind of work where failure isn’t an option and the mission is clear. What that experience gave me, more than anything, was a framework for thinking about critical systems: what they depend on, where they’re vulnerable, and what it actually takes to keep them running.
I think about the grid the same way. Electricity is more than an essential service. It’s the infrastructure that supports everything else: hospitals, water systems, communications networks, manufacturing facilities, and military installations. When it works, most people don’t think about it. When it doesn’t, the consequences are immediate and widespread. That’s why I view grid resilience not simply as an energy issue, but as a national resilience issue.
Today, that resilience is being tested. Utilities are confronting rising demand from data centers, electrification, new manufacturing investments, and other sources of load growth, all while managing infrastructure that was designed for a different era. New generation and transmission will be essential to meeting those needs, but many of those investments require years to permit, finance, and construct.
That reality has elevated the role of demand-side management. The industry often frames reliability and sustainability as competing priorities. In practice, demand-side resources are one of the few tools capable of advancing both. By reducing unnecessary consumption and shifting load away from periods of peak demand, they can strengthen reliability while helping utilities achieve sustainability goals more cost-effectively.
But it’s important to be clear about both what demand-side management can do and what it cannot.
Where Demand Management Genuinely Helps
The strongest case for demand-side work is speed. Large infrastructure projects, including new generation resources, transmission lines, and substation upgrades, can take a decade or more to move from planning to operation. Load growth isn’t waiting. Demand-side programs can often be designed, deployed, and producing measurable results within months rather than years. That matters when utilities are managing reliability pressures in real time.
Energy efficiency reduces the amount of electricity needed in the first place. Demand flexibility changes when electricity is used. Together, they provide utilities and grid operators with additional tools to manage peak demand, defer certain capital investments, and create breathing room while larger infrastructure projects move forward.
Demand-side resources also offer a practical bridge between reliability and sustainability objectives. Every kilowatt-hour that doesn’t need to be generated reduces pressure on the system. In many cases, efficiency improvements can help utilities accommodate growing demand while lowering costs and reducing associated emissions. Those benefits become increasingly valuable as utilities work to balance affordability, reliability, and environmental goals simultaneously.
Some utilities are already treating demand-side resources with the same seriousness as supply-side investments, incorporating energy efficiency and demand flexibility into long-term resource planning. That shift reflects a broader recognition that managing demand is no longer a supplemental strategy. In many territories, it is becoming an essential part of the reliability toolkit.
For utilities facing rising peak loads, interconnection constraints, and increasing pressure to control costs, that approach isn’t simply good policy. It’s good operations.
Where It Falls Short
Demand management is not a substitute for supply. It is a complement to it, and confusing the two creates expectations that no demand-side program can realistically meet.
Large industrial facilities, advanced manufacturing operations, and data centers require dependable, continuous power. Demand flexibility works best for loads that can be shifted or reduced during periods of system stress. It is far less effective for operations where interruptions carry significant operational or financial consequences. Utilities serving these customers still need generation and transmission capacity. Efficiency programs do not eliminate that requirement.
There is also a fairness question the industry continues to navigate. Some demand-side programs may disproportionately benefit customers who have the capital, technology, or flexibility to participate, while broader infrastructure costs remain shared across the entire customer base. Utilities and regulators will need to continue refining program design to ensure benefits are accessible and equitable.
Measurement presents another challenge. Demonstrating that energy savings are real, additional, and persistent requires rigorous evaluation. Reliable outcomes depend on reliable measurement, and not every program is designed with the same level of discipline and accountability.
Scale is a limiting factor as well. Demand-side resources can meaningfully reduce growth in electricity consumption and help manage system peaks, but they are unlikely to offset the full magnitude of anticipated load growth on their own. They narrow the gap. They do not close it.
Any honest discussion about grid reliability should begin with that recognition.
What Utilities Are Actually Contending With
The utilities I speak with are not debating whether demand-side resources have value. They do. The challenge is determining how to integrate those resources into planning frameworks that were built for slower demand growth, more predictable consumption patterns, and a clearer separation between the supply side and the demand side of the equation.
That integration requires more than good intentions. It requires data, customer engagement, program infrastructure, and regulatory frameworks that allow demand-side investments to be evaluated alongside supply-side alternatives. In many jurisdictions, those frameworks are still evolving.
Utilities are also grappling with questions of cost allocation, resource adequacy, and long-term planning amid unprecedented uncertainty. The assumptions that guided resource planning for decades are changing. Load forecasts are becoming more dynamic. Customer expectations are rising. The need for flexibility is growing.
Against that backdrop, the most effective strategies are not built around a single solution. They combine new generation, upgraded transmission, demand-side resources, and regulatory structures that support integrated planning. Utilities that are succeeding in this environment are treating demand-side management as a core component of their strategy while remaining realistic about its limitations.
The industry does not have the luxury of choosing between reliability and sustainability. It must deliver both.
Demand-side management will not solve every challenge facing the grid. It cannot replace the need for new generation, upgraded transmission, or continued infrastructure investment. But it can reduce consumption, ease pressure during peak periods, lower emissions, and buy time while larger investments come online. For utilities managing real reliability pressure right now, that’s not a small thing.
The grid is a critical system. Treat it like one, and use every tool available to keep it running.
— Rich McBee is president and CEO of CLEAResult , North America’s largest provider of energy efficiency, energy transition, and energy sustainability services.
